Chapter overview

Study Post-Sangam Tamil Literature through the 11–6–1 Pathinenkilkanakku structure, the Great and Minor Epics, other narrative and grammatical works, and Jain–Buddhist literary contribution. Detailed Thirukkural study remains in Chapters 9–16.

Post-Sangam Period: Scope and Classification

The Sangam-Maruvia phase marks a transition towards ethical collections, narrative epics and Jain–Buddhist intellectual traditions.

Period and Classification

The period following classical Sangam literature is commonly called the Sangam-Maruvia period or Post-Sangam period.

Tamil literary history generally places the core Pathinenkilkanakku works between approximately 300 CE and 600 CE.

The major literary groups covered in this chapter are:

  • Pathinenkilkanakku
  • Five Great Epics
  • Five Minor Epics
  • Perunkathai
  • Muttollayiram
  • Iraiyanar Akapporul

The dates of individual epics remain debated. Some epics belong to later centuries but are conventionally studied as part of the post-Sangam epic tradition.

Literary Classification
  • Pathinenkilkanakku — eighteen shorter works, generally placed in the core 300–600 CE phase.
  • Five Great Epics — major narrative poems with Jain and Buddhist associations.
  • Five Minor Epics — chiefly connected with Jain literary traditions.
  • Other works — Perunkathai, Muttollayiram and Iraiyanar Akapporul.
  • Individual epic dates remain debated; some works conventionally grouped here belong to later centuries.
Pathinenkilkanakku: Ethical Works

The eleven ethical works use concise Venpa-based instruction to organise conduct, learning, self-control, charity and social responsibility.

Eighteen Minor Works

Pathinenkilkanakku means the Eighteen Lower or Minor Works.

The word “minor” refers mainly to the shorter poetic form and later position in literary classification, not to literary quality.

The eighteen works are classified into:

  • Eleven ethical works
  • Six Akam works
  • One Puram work

Most Pathinenkilkanakku works are written in Venpa metre.

Eleven Ethical Works

The eleven ethical works are:

  • Thirukkural
  • Naladiyar
  • Nanmanikkadigai
  • Inna Narpathu
  • Iniyavai Narpathu
  • Tirikatukam
  • Acharakkovai
  • Pazhamozhi Nanuru
  • Sirupanchamulam
  • Muthumozhikanchi
  • Elathi

They are also called Aranoolgal or Neethinoolgal.

Thirukkural

Author: Tiruvalluvar

Other name: Muppal

Number of couplets: 1,330

Sections: Aram, Porul and Inbam

Thirukkural is one of the eleven ethical works of Pathinenkilkanakku.

Its philosophy, secular character, everyday relevance, universal values and political and economic ideas are reserved for Chapters 9–16.

Naladiyar

Authors: Several Jain ascetics

Number of poems: 400

Metre: Venpa

Other names: Naladi Nanuru and Velan Vedam

Each poem contains four lines, giving the work the name Naladiyar.

It is traditionally ranked next to Thirukkural among Tamil ethical works.

Major subjects include:

  • Impermanence of life
  • Renunciation
  • Education
  • Friendship
  • Generosity
  • Self-control
  • Good conduct

Naladiyar is attributed to several poets rather than a single author.

Nanmanikkadigai

Author: Vilambi Naganar

Number of poems: 104 in the traditional count, including invocatory poems

Metre: Venpa

The title means an ornament made of four precious gems.

Each poem generally presents four valuable ethical ideas.

The invocatory verses praise Thirumal, and Vilambi Naganar is therefore associated with Vaishnavism.

Inna Narpathu

Author: Kapilar

Number of principal poems: 40

Form: Venpa

The work lists actions and situations that cause pain or suffering.

Each poem generally identifies four undesirable things.

The author named Kapilar is not securely identifiable with the famous Sangam-age Kapilar.

The text contains an additional invocatory verse in traditional editions.

Iniyavai Narpathu

Author: Poothanchenthanar

Number of principal poems: 40

Form: Venpa

Iniyavai Narpathu lists actions, qualities and experiences considered pleasant or desirable.

Important subjects include:

  • Learning
  • Self-control
  • Good friendship
  • Charity
  • Respect for parents
  • Just governance
  • Freedom from debt

Inna Narpathu explains what should be avoided, while Iniyavai Narpathu explains what should be followed.

Tirikatukam

Author: Nallathanar

Number of poems: 101, including the invocation

Metre: Venpa

The name refers to a medicinal mixture made from:

  • Sukku — dry ginger
  • Milagu — pepper
  • Thippili — long pepper

Each poem generally combines three ethical ideas, just as the medicine contains three ingredients.

The work stresses:

  • Compassion
  • Truthfulness
  • Education
  • Good governance
  • Duties of ministers and envoys
  • Rejection of killing and meat-eating
Sirupanchamulam

Author: Kariyasan

Number of poems: 100 in the traditional text

Metre: Venpa

Sirupanchamulam is the name of a medicine prepared from five roots.

Each poem generally contains five moral instructions.

The work discusses:

  • Charity
  • Education
  • Friendship
  • Family life
  • Assistance to others
  • Avoidance of harmful conduct

Kariyasan is traditionally identified as a Jain scholar and a student of Makkayanar.

Elathi

Author: Kanimethaviyar

Number of principal poems: 80

Metre: Venpa

Elathi is named after a medicinal preparation containing six ingredients:

  • Cardamom
  • Cinnamon
  • Nagakesaram
  • Pepper
  • Long pepper
  • Dry ginger

Each poem generally conveys six ethical ideas.

Kanimethaviyar also composed Thinai Maalai Nootraimbathu.

He is traditionally identified as a Jain scholar and an expert in astrology.

Acharakkovai

Author: Peruvayin Mulliyar

Number of poems: 100

Metre: Venpa

Acharakkovai deals with personal and social conduct.

It contains instructions relating to:

  • Cleanliness
  • Food habits
  • Hospitality
  • Respect for elders
  • Conduct before teachers and rulers
  • Daily discipline
  • Speech and behaviour

CICT notes that it incorporates ideas found in Sanskrit ethical and Smriti traditions.

Pazhamozhi Nanuru

Author: Munrurai Araiyanar

Number of poems: 400

Metre: Venpa

Each poem contains or concludes with a traditional proverb.

The proverbs are explained through:

  • Historical incidents
  • Royal stories
  • Social situations
  • Animal behaviour
  • Everyday experience

Pazhamozhi Nanuru preserves a large body of early Tamil proverbial tradition.

Munrurai Araiyanar is generally associated with Jainism.

Muthumozhikanchi

Author: Madurai Kudalur Kilar

Number of maxims: 100

Arrangement: Ten groups of ten

Muthumozhi means an ancient saying or mature maxim.

Kanchi refers to a literary mode associated with impermanence.

The work contains concise statements on:

  • Education
  • Conduct
  • Wisdom
  • Social honour
  • Impermanence
  • Self-discipline

It is organised into ten sections, each containing ten short maxims.

Pathinenkilkanakku: Akam and Puram Works

Six Akam texts continue Thinai conventions, while Kalavazhi Narpathu alone represents Puram battlefield poetry.

Akam Texts of Pathinenkilkanakku

The six Akam works are:

  • Kar Narpathu
  • Ainthinai Aimpathu
  • Thinai Mozhi Aimpathu
  • Ainthinai Ezhupathu
  • Thinai Maalai Nootraimbathu
  • Kainnilai

They continue the five-landscape love conventions of Sangam Akam poetry.

Kar Narpathu

Author: Madurai Kannan Koothanar

Number of poems: 40

Thinai: Mullai

Metre: Venpa

The rainy season appears in every poem.

The heroine waits for the hero who has gone on a military or royal duty and promised to return during the rains.

The work contains references to:

  • Separation
  • Patient waiting
  • Rain clouds
  • The return of the hero
  • Consolation offered by the friend

The author’s name is also written as Madurai Kannan Koothanar or Madurai Kannan Koothan.

Ainthinai Aimpathu

Author: Maran Poraiyanar

Number of poems: 50

Metre: Venpa

The work contains ten poems for each of the five landscapes.

The order followed is:

  • Mullai
  • Kurinji
  • Marutham
  • Palai
  • Neithal

Its opening poem refers to Thirumal, Murugan and Siva.

Thinai Mozhi Aimpathu

Author: Kannan Senthanar

Number of poems: 50

Metre: Venpa

It contains ten poems for each of the five Akam landscapes.

The order is:

  • Kurinji
  • Palai
  • Mullai
  • Marutham
  • Neithal

The work presents the characteristic speech and emotional situations associated with each landscape.

Ainthinai Ezhupathu

Author: Muvathiyar

Original number: 70 poems

Surviving number: 66 poems

Metre: Venpa

Four poems have been lost.

Each of the five landscapes was originally allotted fourteen poems.

An invocation to Vinayaka occurs in the present text, but scholars generally regard it as a later addition because Vinayaka worship became prominent in Tamil literature after the period assigned to the original work.

Thinai Maalai Nootraimbathu

Author: Kanimethaviyar

Title count: 150 poems

Present text: 153 poems

It is the largest Akam work in Pathinenkilkanakku.

The arrangement is:

  • Kurinji
  • Neithal
  • Palai
  • Mullai
  • Marutham

The three poems exceeding the title count are generally treated as additional verses.

Kanimethaviyar also composed Elathi.

Kainnilai

Author: Pullangadanar

Number of poems: 60

Arrangement: Twelve poems for each Thinai

Metre: Venpa

The five landscapes appear in the order:

  • Kurinji
  • Palai
  • Mullai
  • Marutham
  • Neithal

Eighteen poems survive in a damaged or incomplete form.

The author is identified more fully as Pullangadanar, son of Kavithiyar of Nallur in Mullinadu.

Kalavazhi Narpathu

Author: Poigaiyar

Subject: Battlefield poetry

Metre: Venpa

Traditional count: Forty poems, with an additional invocation in some editions

The work describes the battle between:

  • Chola Sengannan
  • Chera Kanaikkal Irumporai

The battle is associated with Kazhumalam.

Chola Sengannan defeated and imprisoned the Chera ruler.

Literary tradition states that Poigaiyar composed Kalavazhi Narpathu and secured the Chera ruler’s release.

Elephants and the destruction of the battlefield receive prominent description.

Kalavazhi Narpathu is the only Puram work among the eighteen Pathinenkilkanakku texts.

Five Great Epics: Overview and Classification

The Five Great Epics expanded Tamil narrative poetry through justice, compassion, heroic adventure, renunciation and religious debate.

Aimperumkappiyam

The Five Great Tamil Epics are:

  • Silappadikaram
  • Manimekalai
  • Civaka Cintamani
  • Valayapathi
  • Kundalakesi

Silappadikaram and Manimekalai are available substantially in complete form.

Civaka Cintamani is also preserved.

Valayapathi and Kundalakesi survive only through fragments and quotations.

Silappadikaram, Manimekalai and Civaka Cintamani survive substantially, while Valayapathi and Kundalakesi survive through fragments and quotations.

  • Jain associations — Civaka Cintamani, Valayapathi and, by traditional attribution, Silappadikaram.
  • Buddhist associations — Manimekalai and Kundalakesi.
  • Silappadikaram and Manimekalai share a continuous narrative world.
  • The epics expanded Tamil narrative poetry and preserved religious and philosophical debate.
Silappadikaram

Silappadikaram combines the anklet narrative, political justice, music, dance and Pattini tradition across three regional Kandams.

Basic Facts

Author: Ilango Adigal

Meaning: The story of the anklet

Status: First extant Tamil epic

Divisions: Three Kandams

Number of Kathais: 30

The three Kandams are:

  • Puhar Kandam
  • Madurai Kandam
  • Vanchi Kandam

The three divisions are associated respectively with the Chola, Pandya and Chera regions.

Main Characters
  • Kannagi
  • Kovalan
  • Madhavi
  • Manimekalai
  • Kavunti Adigal
  • Pandya Nedunchezhiyan
  • Pandima Devi
  • Cheran Senguttuvan

Kovalan leaves Kannagi and lives with the dancer Madhavi.

After losing his wealth, he returns to Kannagi and travels with her to Madurai.

Kovalan is wrongly executed for allegedly stealing the Pandya queen’s anklet.

Anklet Evidence

The Pandya queen’s anklet contained pearls.

Kannagi’s anklet contained rubies or precious red stones.

Kannagi broke her anklet before the Pandya king and proved that Kovalan had been wrongly executed.

The Pandya king died after realising the miscarriage of justice.

Kannagi then cursed and burned Madurai.

Three Central Messages

Silappadikaram states three principal ideas:

  • Political injustice is punished by Aram
  • A chaste woman is honoured by society
  • Fate produces its inevitable result

These are traditionally expressed as:

  • Arasiyal Pizhaithorkku Aram Kootru
  • Uraisal Pathiniyai Uyarnthor Ethal
  • Oozhvinai Uruthu Vanthu Oottum
Literary Features

Silappadikaram is described as:

  • Muthamizh Kappiyam
  • Uraiyidaiyitta Paattudai Cheyyul
  • A narrative combining poetry, prose, music and drama

Muthamizh refers to:

  • Iyal — literature
  • Isai — music
  • Natakam — drama

Unlike many royal epics, its central characters belong to a merchant family.

It is therefore frequently called a Kudimakkal Kappiyam, or epic of ordinary citizens.

Important Dances and Musical References

Silappadikaram contains detailed references to:

  • Arangetru Kathai
  • Aychiyar Kuravai
  • Kunra Kuravai
  • Vettuva Vari
  • Kanal Vari
  • Musical instruments
  • Dance forms
  • Pann system

Madhavi is presented as an accomplished dancer and musician.

Pattini Tradition

The Vanchi Kandam connects Cheran Senguttuvan with:

  • A northern expedition
  • Bringing a stone from the Himalayas
  • Consecrating Kannagi as Pattini
  • Participation of the Sri Lankan ruler Gajabahu in the ceremony

The account is part of the epic tradition and is also used in discussions of the Gajabahu synchronism.

Manimekalai

Manimekalai continues the Silappadikaram world through Buddhist compassion, renunciation, philosophical debate and the removal of hunger.

Basic Facts

Author: Seethalai Sattanar

Religion: Buddhism

Number of Kathais: 30

Heroine: Manimekalai

Manimekalai is the daughter of:

  • Kovalan
  • Madhavi

It continues the narrative world of Silappadikaram and is therefore called its sequel or twin epic.

It is the most complete surviving Tamil Buddhist epic.

Main Story

Prince Udayakumaran falls in love with Manimekalai.

Manimekalai rejects marriage and worldly life and becomes a Buddhist nun.

Important characters and places include:

  • Madhavi
  • Sudhamathi
  • Udayakumaran
  • Aravana Adigal
  • Aputhiran
  • Puhar
  • Manipallavam
  • Vanchi
  • Kanchi
Amudha Surabhi

Manimekalai receives the inexhaustible food bowl called:

Amudha Surabhi

The vessel provides food continuously to the hungry.

It had earlier been associated with Aputhiran.

The work presents the removal of hunger as a supreme form of charity.

Manimekalai also converts a prison into a charitable institution where prisoners are fed.

Buddhist Elements

Manimekalai discusses:

  • Impermanence
  • Karma
  • Rebirth
  • Compassion
  • Renunciation
  • Buddhist logic
  • Different Indian philosophical schools
  • Rejection of killing
  • Rejection of intoxicating liquor

The later portions contain extensive religious and philosophical debates.

Manipallavam

Manipallavam is an island visited by Manimekalai.

It is associated with:

  • A Buddhist pedestal
  • Knowledge of previous births
  • Amudha Surabhi
  • Maritime connections with Sri Lanka

Manipallavam is traditionally identified with an island near northern Sri Lanka.

Civaka Cintamani, Valayapathi and Kundalakesi

These three Great Epics contrast substantial Jain narrative survival with two fragmentary works reconstructed through quotations and tradition.

Civaka Cintamani

A Jain epic centred on Civakan, combining heroic achievement, courtly life and final renunciation.

Basic Facts

Author: Tiruttakkatevar

Religion: Jainism

Hero: Civakan

Divisions: 13 Ilambakams

Number of verses: 3,145

Metre: Predominantly Viruttam

Tiruttakkatevar was a Jain ascetic.

Civaka Cintamani became an important model for later Tamil epic composition.

Story and Alternative Name

The epic describes:

  • Birth and upbringing of Civakan
  • Education and martial training
  • Military victories
  • Medical and artistic skills
  • Marriages
  • Recovery of his kingdom
  • Final renunciation

Because Civakan marries several women, the work is popularly called:

Mananool

The final Ilambakam concerns his renunciation and liberation.

Literary Importance

Civaka Cintamani expanded the use of Viruttam metre in long narrative poetry.

It influenced later epic poets, including Kamban.

The text combines:

  • Heroic adventure
  • Love
  • Court life
  • Detailed descriptions
  • Jain ethics
  • Final renunciation

Its luxurious descriptions are followed by the hero’s rejection of worldly life.

Valayapathi

A fragmentary Jain epic known mainly through quotations and later testimony.

Basic Facts

Religion: Jainism

Author: Unknown

Status: Lost except for fragments

The original story, number of sections and date are uncertain.

Available verses survive through:

  • Grammatical commentaries
  • Literary anthologies
  • Quotations in later texts

The surviving verses emphasise:

  • Jain ethics
  • Renunciation
  • Impermanence
  • Family life
  • Value of children
  • Criticism of sensual attachment
Lost Manuscript Tradition

U. V. Swaminatha Iyer stated that he had once seen a Valayapathi manuscript at the Tiruvavaduthurai Adheenam.

When he later searched for it, the manuscript could not be found.

Valayapathi is therefore one of the important lost works of Tamil literary history.

Kundalakesi

A fragmentary Buddhist epic centred on a merchant’s daughter who becomes a renunciant and teacher.

Basic Facts

Author: Nathakuthanar or Nagakuthanar

Religion: Buddhism

Status: Survives only in fragments

Heroine: Kundalakesi

The name Kundalakesi refers to the heroine’s curly hair.

The text survives mainly through quotations in later commentaries and works written against it.

Story

Kundalakesi is traditionally described as the daughter of a wealthy merchant.

She falls in love with a condemned robber and secures his release.

After marriage, the husband attempts to kill her.

Kundalakesi kills him in self-defence and later renounces worldly life.

She studies different philosophies and becomes a Buddhist teacher.

Five Minor Epics

The Five Minor Epics are linked mainly with Jain narrative, ethical instruction, debate and renunciation.

Ainchirukappiyam

The Five Minor Tamil Epics are:

  • Neelakesi
  • Chulamani
  • Yasodhara Kaviyam
  • Udayana Kumara Kaviyam
  • Nagakumara Kaviyam

All five are associated with Jain literary traditions.

Neelakesi

Religion: Jainism

Author: Unknown

Neelakesi is a religious and philosophical debate text.

Its heroine travels to different places and debates with followers of:

  • Buddhism
  • Ajivika tradition
  • Samkhya
  • Vedic schools
  • Other philosophical systems

It directly challenges the doctrines associated with Kundalakesi.

Chulamani

Author: Tholamozhi Thevar

Religion: Jainism

Chulamani is one of the best-preserved minor epics.

It contains:

  • Royal history
  • Battles
  • Marriage
  • Jain ethical teachings
  • Renunciation

The work is known for polished language, elaborate descriptions and Viruttam metre.

Yasodhara Kaviyam

Religion: Jainism

Central figure: Yasodhara

The work emphasises:

  • Non-violence
  • Karma
  • Consequences of animal sacrifice
  • Renunciation

It strongly condemns killing performed in the name of religious sacrifice.

Udayana Kumara Kaviyam

Religion: Jainism

Central figure: Udayana

Only part of the work survives.

It belongs to the wider narrative tradition concerning King Udayana.

Nagakumara Kaviyam

Religion: Jainism

Central figure: Nagakumara

The epic describes royal life, pleasure, ethical instruction and eventual renunciation.

Its author is not securely known.

Perunkathai, Muttollayiram and Iraiyanar Akapporul

These works represent extended narrative, dynastic praise and Akam grammatical commentary outside the principal epic lists.

Perunkathai

Author: Kongu Velir

Religion of author: Jainism

Central figure: Udayana

Status: Incomplete

Perunkathai belongs to the Brihatkatha narrative tradition.

Kongu Velir adapted the story into Tamil through an earlier northern version.

The work contains:

  • Royal adventures
  • Love and marriage
  • Political intrigue
  • Travel
  • Music
  • Mechanical devices
  • Jain cultural influence

The beginning and ending portions have been lost.

Muttollayiram

Author: Unknown

Metre: Venpa

Subject: Chera, Chola and Pandya rulers

One interpretation of the title states that the original work contained:

  • 900 poems on the Cheras
  • 900 poems on the Cholas
  • 900 poems on the Pandyas

This would give a total of 2,700 poems.

Only a small portion survives through Purathirattu and quotations in later commentaries.

Editions differ in the number of surviving poems, commonly presenting approximately 108 or 109 core poems, while some later editions add further verses from commentaries.

Content of Muttollayiram

The surviving poems describe:

  • Bravery of the Muvendar
  • War elephants
  • Cavalry
  • Royal generosity
  • Capital cities
  • Defeat of enemy kingdoms
  • Women’s one-sided love for kings

The kings are generally identified through dynastic titles rather than individual personal names.

Muttollayiram contributed to the later development of Ula literature.

Iraiyanar Akapporul

Other name: Iraiyanar Kalaviyal

Number of sutras: 60

Subject: Akam grammar, especially Kalavu

The sutras are traditionally attributed to Iraiyanar.

The famous prose commentary is associated with Nakkirar.

The commentary discusses:

  • Akam conventions
  • Kalavu and Karpu
  • Poetic traditions
  • Pandya patronage
  • The traditional account of the three Tamil Sangams

The commentary is one of the earliest major examples of Tamil prose commentary.

Jain Contribution to Tamil Literature

Jain scholars shaped ethical verse, epic narrative, grammar, debate and disciplined reflection on non-violence and renunciation.

Important Jain Works

Jain-associated works include:

  • Naladiyar
  • Pazhamozhi Nanuru
  • Sirupanchamulam
  • Elathi
  • Thinai Maalai Nootraimbathu
  • Silappadikaram, according to the traditional identification of Ilango Adigal
  • Civaka Cintamani
  • Valayapathi
  • Neelakesi
  • Chulamani
  • Yasodhara Kaviyam
  • Udayana Kumara Kaviyam
  • Nagakumara Kaviyam
  • Perunkathai

Major Jain literary themes include:

  • Non-violence
  • Vegetarianism
  • Karma
  • Impermanence
  • Renunciation
  • Ethical discipline

The precise religious identity of some early authors remains a matter of scholarly interpretation.

Buddhist Contribution and Religious Debates

Buddhist Tamil works foreground compassion, hunger, impermanence, rebirth and philosophical debate, especially through Manimekalai and Kundalakesi.

Important Buddhist Works

The principal Buddhist Tamil epics are:

  • Manimekalai
  • Kundalakesi

Manimekalai survives substantially in full.

Kundalakesi survives only in fragments.

Important Buddhist literary themes include:

  • Compassion
  • Feeding the hungry
  • Impermanence
  • Karma and rebirth
  • Renunciation
  • Philosophical debate
Kundalakesi and Neelakesi

Kundalakesi represents Buddhist debate literature, while the Jain Neelakesi responds polemically to its doctrines. Together they show competing philosophical traditions in Tamil literary history.

Neelakesi Connection

The Jain epic Neelakesi was written as a polemical response to Buddhist arguments associated with Kundalakesi.

The two works are important examples of religious debate in Tamil literary history.

Rapid Revision and High-Yield Distinctions

The final topic consolidates classifications, medicinal titles, author–work associations, religions, survival status and common comparison traps.

Rapid Revision

  • Ethical works — 11
  • Akam works — 6
  • Puram works — 1

  • Thirukkural — Tiruvalluvar
  • Naladiyar — Jain ascetics
  • Nanmanikkadigai — Vilambi Naganar
  • Inna Narpathu — Kapilar
  • Iniyavai Narpathu — Poothanchenthanar

  • Sirupanchamulam — Kariyasan

Akam Works and Authors
  • Kar Narpathu — Madurai Kannan Koothanar

Medicinal Titles
  • Tirikatukam — three medicinal ingredients — three ideas per poem
  • Sirupanchamulam — five medicinal roots — five ideas per poem
  • Elathi — six medicinal ingredients — six ideas per poem
  • Nanmanikkadigai — four gems — four ideas per poem
Five Great Epics
  • Silappadikaram — Ilango Adigal — Jain association
  • Manimekalai — Seethalai Sattanar — Buddhist

Epic Associations
  • Silappadikaram — anklet, Kannagi and Kovalan

  • Civaka Cintamani — Mananool and Viruttam

  • Kundalakesi — lost Buddhist epic

  • Perunkathai — Kongu Velir and Udayana
High-Yield Distinctions
  • Pathinenmelkanakku consists of Ettuthokai and Pattuppattu; Pathinenkilkanakku consists of the eighteen post-Sangam works.
  • Pathinenkilkanakku contains 11 ethical, 6 Akam and 1 Puram work.
  • Kalavazhi Narpathu is the only Puram work in Pathinenkilkanakku.
  • Kar Narpathu deals only with Mullai Thinai.
  • Thinai Maalai Nootraimbathu is the largest Akam text in Pathinenkilkanakku.
  • Kanimethaviyar wrote both Elathi and Thinai Maalai Nootraimbathu.
  • Silappadikaram contains three Kandams and 30 Kathais.
  • Manimekalai also contains 30 Kathais.
  • Kannagi’s anklet contained rubies; the Pandya queen’s anklet contained pearls.
  • Manimekalai is the daughter of Kovalan and Madhavi.
  • Amudha Surabhi belongs to Manimekalai.
  • Civaka Cintamani contains 13 Ilambakams and 3,145 verses.
  • Valayapathi is Jain; Kundalakesi is Buddhist.
  • Neelakesi is a Jain response to Kundalakesi.
  • Perunkathai was composed by Kongu Velir.
  • Muttollayiram praises all three crowned Tamil dynasties.
  • The commentary on Iraiyanar Akapporul is the main source for the traditional account of the three Tamil Sangams.
  • Complete and fragmentary epics Silappadikaram, Manimekalai and Civaka Cintamani survive substantially; Valayapathi and Kundalakesi are fragmentary.
  • Silappadikaram and Manimekalai Silappadikaram centres on Kannagi and justice; Manimekalai continues the narrative world through Buddhist compassion and renunciation.
  • Perunkathai and Udayana Kumara Kaviyam Both belong to Udayana narrative traditions, but Perunkathai is the larger Tamil adaptation by Kongu Velir.
  • Muttollayiram and Pathitrupathu Muttollayiram praises all three crowned dynasties; Pathitrupathu is devoted to Chera rulers.
  • Iraiyanar Akapporul and Tolkappiyam Iraiyanar Akapporul is a concise Akam grammatical work of sixty sutras; Tolkappiyam is the broader extant grammar and poetics text.
